Numbers.title: Numbers & time
Numbers.subtitle: Numbers, dates, clock times and prices: learn them, then drill them.

cardinals.rule: From 21 on, German says the ones first and the tens second, glued together with und: 21 is ein·und·zwanzig (“one-and-twenty”). Watch the spelling: 16 sechzehn and 17 siebzehn drop letters, and so do 60 sechzig and 70 siebzig. 30 is dreißig with ß. And each number is written as one (sometimes very long) word.
cardinals.hundredNote: 100 can be hundert or einhundert, 1000 can be tausend or eintausend. After the hundreds you just keep going: 101 is hunderteins, 321 is dreihunderteinundzwanzig.
cardinals.converterInvalid: Please type a whole number from 0 to 9999.

ordinals.title: Ordinal numbers 1–31
ordinals.rule: Up to 19, add -te: vierte, fünfte, zehnte. Four like to be different: erste, dritte, siebte, achte. From 20, add -ste: zwanzigste, einunddreißigste. In dates the ordinal needs an adjective ending: -e after der (der dritte), -en after am (am dritten).
ordinals.written: In writing, put a dot after the number: 3. November.

calendar.articleNote: Easy one: all months, weekdays and seasons are masculine. der Januar, der Montag, der Sommer.
calendar.todayNote: The calendar opens on today's date.

clock.hint: Drag the hands on the clock or use the sliders.
clock.noEveryday: In everyday German people count in 5-minute steps. Move the minute to a multiple of 5.
clock.tip: Tricky one: halb means “half before”, so halb drei is 2:30, not 3:30. halb and Viertel vor always look ahead to the next hour.

v2.title: The verb comes second (V2)
v2.body: In a German statement the conjugated verb always takes the second spot. First place can go to the subject or to something else, like the time. If something else goes first, the subject slides in right behind the verb.

question.title: Asking questions
question.body: In a W-question the question word comes first, then the verb, then the subject. In a yes/no question the verb jumps to the very front.

modal-bracket.title: Modal verbs and the sentence frame
modal-bracket.body: The conjugated modal verb sits in position 2. The second verb stays in the infinitive and goes all the way to the end. Together they hug the rest of the sentence like a frame (Satzklammer).

separable-bracket.title: Separable verbs and the sentence frame
separable-bracket.body: In a main clause the verb stem sits in position 2 and the prefix breaks off and goes to the very end. The two parts frame the sentence (Satzklammer).

subordinate-weil.title: weil sends the verb to the end
subordinate-weil.body: After weil you are in a subordinate clause, and the conjugated verb moves to the end of it. A comma separates it from the main clause.

negation-nicht-kein.title: Saying no with nicht and kein
negation-nicht-kein.body: Use kein for a noun that has ein or no article. Use nicht for a verb or the whole sentence; it usually goes near the end.

time-manner-place.title: Time – Manner – Place
time-manner-place.body: When a sentence has several details, the usual order is Time (when), Manner (how), Place (where). The verb still stays in position 2.

Path.title: Your path

articles.title: Articles
articles.desc: Get 5 right in a row in the articles game.
articles.why: Every German noun comes with der, die or das. Learn it together with each word from day one and future you will say thanks.

pronouns.title: Pronouns
pronouns.why: ich, du, er, sie… You need them in every sentence, and the verb ending depends on them.

verbs.title: Verbs
verbs.why: With sein, haben and a handful of common verbs you can already say a lot about yourself.

cases.title: Nominative and accusative
cases.why: Nominative or accusative decides whether it's der or den. Crack this and your sentences start sounding right.

vocabulary.title: Vocabulary
vocabulary.desc: Add 10 words to your review deck.
vocabulary.why: Words in your review deck come back just before you'd forget them. Your memory does the rest.

numbers.title: Numbers and time
numbers.desc: Practise until the ring is half full.
numbers.why: Prices, times, dates and phone numbers pop up in every conversation, and in the exam.

modal.title: Modal verbs
modal.why: können, müssen, wollen: say what you can, must and want to do.

dialogues.title: Dialogues
dialogues.why: See what you've learnt in real everyday situations, and play one of the roles yourself.

reading.title: Reading
reading.why: Short texts that train exactly what the A1 reading test asks for.

sentences.title: Sentences
sentences.why: Get a feel for where the verb goes: second place, or at the very end when there's a second verb.

review.title: Review
review.why: A few minutes of review a day moves words into your long-term memory for good.

exam.title: Practice exam
exam.why: See where you stand before the real thing, part by part. You've got this.

Nudge.label: Save your progress
Nudge.title: Don't lose your progress
Nudge.text: Right now everything you've learnt lives only in this browser. A free account keeps it safe and takes it to every device.

sections.h: Using the app without an account
p: You can use every part of the app without an account. Your progress is then saved only in your browser's local storage on your device. It is never sent to us.
We do not use analytics, advertising or tracking cookies.

sections.h: What we store when you create an account
p: Your full name, your email address and your password. The password is stored only as a salted scrypt hash; nobody can read it.
If you sign in with Google: your Google account ID, name and email address as Google provides them.
Your learning progress (review cards, quiz and exercise results, streak days, settings), so it can be synced between your devices.
We keep short-lived counters of sign-in and sign-up attempts per email and IP address to protect accounts against password guessing. They expire after at most one hour.
We process this data to provide the account and sync service you asked for (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR) and to keep the service secure (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR).
When you sign in, we set one cookie that keeps you signed in, plus security cookies used during sign-in. They are strictly necessary for the account and are not used for tracking.

Hosting: Vercel Inc. Database: Neon (via Vercel). Password-reset emails: Resend. Optional sign-in: Google. These providers may process data outside the EU, including in the USA, under the EU Standard Contractual Clauses or the EU–US Data Privacy Framework.
Until you delete your account. Password-reset links expire after one hour.

You can delete your account and all its data at any time on the account page. You also have the right to access, correct, restrict or export your data, to object, and to complain to a data protection authority. To use these rights, contact us at the address above.
